summary: Defines EAP-TLS, an EAP method that uses TLS for certificate-based mutual authentication and key derivation. It builds on the EAP framework of RFC 3748. It replaces RFC 2716 and is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: EAP-TLS lets a device and an authentication server check each other's certificates during a network-access exchange. They also derive keys that the lower network layer can use.

questions: how does eap-tls authenticate both sides
subtitle: How EAP carries a TLS certificate exchange so a device and network can authenticate each other and derive keys.

tldr.problem: The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) needs methods that can authenticate both the peer and the network and produce keying material.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-TLS carries TLS handshake records inside EAP packets. Certificates support authentication, and the TLS master secret is used to derive the Master Session Key and Extended Master Session Key.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5216 obsoletes RFC 2716 and defines EAP Type 13. It has been updated by RFC 8996, RFC 9190 and RFC 9965, so its TLS requirements must be read with those updates.

today: RFC 5216 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2716. It has been updated by RFC 8996, RFC 9190 and RFC 9965; read those updates with this specification.

sections.title: Why EAP Uses TLS
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is a framework for authentication methods used with link layers such as PPP and IEEE 802 networks. RFC 5216 defines EAP-TLS, which uses Transport Layer Security (TLS) for certificate-based mutual authentication and key derivation.

The peer responds to the authenticator, which starts EAP. An EAP server terminates the method with the peer; it may be part of the authenticator or a separate backend server that receives passed-through EAP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP is a way for a network to use different methods to check identity. EAP-TLS uses certificates and TLS so both the device and the server can prove who they are.

sections.title: The Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
After the identity exchange, the EAP server sends an EAP-TLS Start request. The peer answers with a TLS client_hello. The server replies with its TLS negotiation and certificate, and may request a peer certificate; the peer then sends its certificate and the remaining handshake messages when requested.

The peers verify the authentication information and finish the TLS exchange before EAP reports success. A resumed TLS session can shorten the exchange: after the server's server_hello, the parties exchange change_cipher_spec and finished messages rather than repeating the full certificate exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The server starts the TLS exchange, and the peer responds. They exchange certificates and handshake messages, then EAP reports success if authentication completes.

sections.title: Optional Identity Privacy
sections.content:
By default, the peer's identity may appear in the initial EAP identity response and in its certificate. Optional privacy support lets the peer use an anonymous Network Access Identifier (NAI) first and send its certificate after TLS provides confidentiality.

A privacy-configured peer initially answers the certificate request with an empty certificate list. A privacy-capable server continues the exchange and requests a certificate again inside the protected session. A peer should use privacy only on networks known to support it, because a server without privacy support may treat the empty first certificate as an error.
sections.plainLanguage: Optional privacy support hides the peer's name during the early exchange. The peer sends its certificate only after TLS protects the conversation, and the server must support this procedure.

sections.title: EAP-TLS Packets and Flags
sections.content:
EAP-TLS Request and Response packets carry the EAP code, identifier, length and Type, followed by a Flags octet and TLS data. Type 13 identifies EAP-TLS. The Request identifier changes for each request, and the Response repeats the identifier of the request it answers.

The flags include L for a following TLS Message Length field, M when more fragments follow, and S for the server's Start message. Reserved flag bits are sent as zero and ignored when received. Data beyond the packet's declared length is link-layer padding and must be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each EAP-TLS packet has labels that identify its type, match replies to requests and describe fragments. The TLS handshake itself travels in the packet's data.

sections.title: Fragmenting Large TLS Messages
sections.content:
TLS messages can exceed the size an EAP packet or RADIUS packet can carry, so EAP-TLS implementations must fragment and reassemble them. The first fragment includes the total TLS message length, and every fragment except the last sets the More Fragments flag.

The receiver acknowledges each fragment before the sender continues. EAP identifiers provide sequencing, so no fragment-offset field is needed. To limit reassembly resource use and denial-of-service risk, the RFC suggests that an implementation may set a maximum message group size, with 64 KB given as a reasonable example.
sections.plainLanguage: If the TLS exchange is too large for one EAP packet, EAP-TLS divides it into pieces. The receiver acknowledges each piece before the next one arrives.

sections.title: Keys and Certificate Identities
sections.content:
EAP-TLS derives exported keying material from the TLS master secret using the TLS pseudo-random function. It produces a Master Session Key (MSK), an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) and an initialization vector. The lower layer determines how these values are used.

The MSK is split into two 32-octet keys, one for peer-to-authenticator traffic and one for authenticator-to-peer traffic. The peer and server identities come from certificate subject information or, when present, subjectAltName. The initial EAP identity is not necessarily the same as the certificate identity and should not be treated as authenticated if they differ.
sections.plainLanguage: After TLS succeeds, both sides derive keys from the shared session secret. The certificates provide the identities that EAP-TLS uses for the peer and server.

sections.title: Certificate Checks and Packet Risks
sections.content:
Peers and servers must authorize the identities in the certificates and support certificate revocation lists; the RFC also recommends support for OCSP. A peer may lack Internet access before authentication, so it must also support checking revocation after connectivity becomes available.

The EAP header fields, Type and Flags are not integrity-protected by TLS. The RFC warns that unchecked extra data can cause buffer overruns and that changing the Type can redirect negotiation toward another TLS-based EAP method or a weaker choice. Implementations need to check packet lengths and protect method selection.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificates need authorization and revocation checks. Some packet labels are not protected by TLS, so implementations must check them carefully to prevent malformed packets and unwanted method changes.
